title: SNMP and Syslog: Giving the AV Network a Memory
description: Use polling, traps and timestamped logs to diagnose AV failures before the evidence disappears.
markdown:
## Why an AV engineer should care

A decoder goes black twice a week. Rebooting fixes it. Everyone blames the network, but the switch looks perfectly healthy when you inspect it.

The problem is not necessarily the network. The problem is that you arrived after the evidence disappeared.

SNMP and syslog let switches—and some AV devices—record what happened before anyone opened the support ticket. Used properly, they can reveal a marginal fiber link, exhausted PoE budget, congested port, overheating switch or endpoint that keeps restarting.

### Today’s objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

- Explain agents, managers, MIBs and OIDs without mystical hand-waving.
- Distinguish SNMP polling, traps and syslog.
- Read traffic, error and discard counters correctly.
- Define a practical monitoring package for an AV network.
- Secure SNMP without becoming a full-time network administrator.

---

## 1. What SNMP actually does

**SNMP** means **Simple Network Management Protocol**. The name is misleading: the protocol is fairly simple, but the surrounding terminology is impressively determined to prevent human understanding.

There are two main participants:

- The **agent** runs inside the switch, UPS, PDU or AV product.
- The **manager**, commonly called an **NMS**, asks agents for information and saves the answers.

An NMS might be PRTG, LibreNMS, SolarWinds, Zabbix or another monitoring platform.

The agent exposes information through a **MIB**, or Management Information Base. Think of a MIB as a structured dictionary describing what information a product can report.

An **OID**, or Object Identifier, is the address of one particular item in that dictionary.

For example, an OID might represent:

- Port operating state
- Bytes received
- Input errors
- Temperature
- System uptime
- PoE power consumption

The standardized Interfaces MIB includes familiar measurements such as 64-bit octet counters, errors, discards and multicast packets. Vendor MIBs extend this with manufacturer-specific information such as stack health, PoE details or optical transceiver measurements. ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2863.html)) Important distinction: **the MIB is not the historical database**. It defines what the device can report. The monitoring server builds history by asking repeatedly and storing the answers.

---

## 2. Polling: “How are you doing right now?”

During polling, the NMS periodically requests values from the agent.

A reasonable interval might be:

- 60 seconds for important AV endpoints and uplinks
- 5 minutes for temperature and other slowly changing conditions
- Faster only when there is a specific reason

The NMS can graph those answers over hours, days or months.

This is far more useful than ping. Ping tells you:

> This address answered me just now.

SNMP can tell you:

> The port remained up, but received 4,000 errors during the blackout, its optical receive level has been drifting downward, and the switch has not rebooted.

### Counters versus gauges

A **gauge** is a current reading: temperature, fan speed or instantaneous PoE draw.

A **counter** generally increases until the device restarts or the counter wraps. Traffic counters therefore do not directly say “this port is using 600 Mbps.” The NMS calculates a rate:


```text
Octets/s = (new octet counter − old octet counter) / elapsed seconds
Bits/s = octets/s × 8
```


Use 64-bit **high-capacity counters** on gigabit and faster interfaces. Their standard names include `ifHCInOctets` and `ifHCOutOctets`; the “HC” means high capacity. The older 32-bit counters can wrap surprisingly quickly on a busy link. ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2863.html)) Discard a rate sample that spans a counter reset or discontinuity rather than treating it as real traffic. Standard sysUpTime measures the SNMP management subsystem: a reset can mean the agent restarted, not necessarily the whole switch. Use vendor device-uptime measurements and correlated syslog where available to confirm a chassis reboot.

Always monitor device uptime as well. A counter returning to zero may indicate miraculous network healing—or merely that the switch rebooted.

---

## 3. Errors and discards are not the same thing

These two categories are especially useful to AV troubleshooting.

**Errors** mean the switch could not properly receive or transmit something. Input CRC/FCS errors commonly point toward:

- Cabling or termination trouble
- Dirty or marginal fiber
- Defective SFPs
- Electrical interference
- Failing hardware

**Discards** mean a packet may have arrived intact but was deliberately dropped. Common causes include:

- Congested queues
- Insufficient egress bandwidth
- Buffer exhaustion
- Policy or filtering behavior
- Bursts exceeding what the port can forward

Therefore:

- Rising errors suggest investigating the physical path.
- Rising discards suggest investigating traffic load, oversubscription and QoS.
- Neither counter, by itself, proves a root cause.

The standard interface MIB deliberately maintains separate error and discard counters. ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2863.html))

---

## 4. Traps and informs: “Something just happened!”

Polling makes the manager ask questions. A **trap** lets the device initiate a message when an event occurs.

Useful notifications include:

- Port went down or came up
- Switch restarted
- Power supply or fan failed
- Temperature crossed a threshold
- PoE overload or denial occurred
- Stack membership changed
- Optical power crossed an alarm threshold
- Authentication failed

A trap is normally **unconfirmed**: the device sends it without requiring an acknowledgment. It can be lost.

An **inform** is a confirmed notification. The receiver acknowledges it, and the sender may retry if no acknowledgment arrives. Not every AV-adjacent product supports informs, so check the platform. The SNMP architecture formally distinguishes unconfirmed traps from confirmed informs. ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3413.html)) This is why a solid system uses both:

- Polling supplies state and trends.
- Traps or informs provide immediate event notification.

A trap alone can disappear. Polling alone can miss a ten-second failure between samples.

---

## 5. Syslog supplies the story

**Syslog** is a separate event-message system. A device pushes timestamped messages to a syslog collector.

SNMP might report:

> Interface 48 is down.

Syslog might report:

> Interface ethernet 1/1/48 changed to down at 14:32:07.

Depending on the switch, another message might identify a PoE fault, spanning-tree transition, authentication failure or transceiver alarm.

Syslog messages contain a severity numbered from 0 through 7:

| Number | Severity |
|---:|---|
| 0 | Emergency |
| 1 | Alert |
| 2 | Critical |
| 3 | Error |
| 4 | Warning |
| 5 | Notice |
| 6 | Informational |
| 7 | Debug |

Lower numbers represent greater severity. Vendor choices about which events receive which severity can vary, so do not assume every “warning” deserves an emergency service call. ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5424)) Configure NTP before trusting any logs. If the switch, decoder and monitoring server disagree about the time, correlating events becomes detective work performed by three witnesses who own different clocks.

Also send logs to a remote collector. Local switch logs are often small and may disappear during the very reboot you are investigating.

---

## 6. What BMT should actually monitor

A practical AV monitoring standard does not need 4,000 reassuring green dots.

For every managed AV switch, start with:

- System uptime
- CPU, memory and temperature
- Power-supply and fan state
- Total PoE budget and consumption
- Uplink operating state and negotiated speed
- Inbound and outbound traffic rate
- Interface errors and discards
- Link-state changes
- Fiber DOM readings where available

For important endpoint ports, add:

- Endpoint port state
- PoE draw and PoE fault events
- Traffic rate
- Errors and discards
- Frequent up/down transitions

For multicast networks, vendor MIBs may also expose IGMP groups, querier status and multicast counters. Availability varies by platform. SNMP cannot retrieve information that the manufacturer’s agent never exposes.

### Security baseline

SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c use community strings and do not provide modern authentication and encryption. Prefer **SNMPv3 using authentication and privacy**, commonly described as `authPriv`. SNMPv3’s User-based Security Model supports message authentication and protection from disclosure. ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3414.html)) BMT’s normal specification should require:

- A read-only SNMPv3 user
- Authentication and encryption using current algorithms supported by the product
- Access restricted to the monitoring server’s IP
- SNMP limited to the management network
- No default `public` or `private` communities
- Write access disabled unless specifically required and documented

Monitoring generally uses UDP 161. Notifications commonly go to UDP 162. Those ports should not be casually exposed outside the management boundary.

---

## 7. Two real AV examples

### Example 1: Intermittent AVoIP receiver blackouts

Several decoders occasionally lose video, but the problem is gone when the technician arrives.

Monitor the decoder ports and switch uplinks for:

- Link changes
- Traffic rates
- Errors and discards
- Switch uptime
- Fiber DOM receive and transmit power
- Transceiver-temperature and threshold alarms
- Traps and syslog events

If optical receive power approaches its alarm threshold while CRC errors rise, investigate the fiber, connectors and SFP.

If the port remains up with clean optics and zero errors, but discards spike during the failure, investigate congestion, multicast flooding and queue behavior.

If all switch evidence remains clean, that does not prove the network innocent—but it justifies moving the investigation toward the encoder, decoder, firmware or application layer.

### Example 2: A PoE camera keeps disappearing

A PTZ camera randomly reboots during meetings.

Compare:

- Camera uptime, if exposed
- Switch uptime
- PoE wattage
- Port link transitions
- PoE denial, overload or restart events
- Syslog messages at the failure time

If the switch remains up but the camera uptime resets immediately after a PoE fault, the power path becomes the prime suspect.

If the entire switch uptime resets, investigate the switch power supply, UPS or upstream electrical system.

Polling might miss a very short event. The trap or syslog message may preserve it.

---

## Practical exercise

Choose one switch uplink and one PoE AV endpoint. Record:

1. Port name and its corresponding drawing/equipment label  
2. Link state and speed  
3. Current traffic rate  
4. Error and discard counters  
5. Switch and endpoint uptime  
6. DOM readings for fiber, if applicable  
7. PoE draw for the endpoint  

During an approved test window, disconnect and reconnect the endpoint. Confirm whether the monitoring system receives a link notification and a syslog message.

The real test is not whether the dashboard turns red. It is whether someone can reconstruct the event afterward.

## Compact glossary

- **SNMP:** Protocol for reading and sometimes changing managed-device information.
- **NMS:** Network Management System—the collector and dashboard.
- **Agent:** SNMP software running on the monitored device.
- **MIB:** Definition of the managed information a device can expose.
- **OID:** Address of one specific managed value.
- **Poll:** Manager-initiated request for current information.
- **Trap:** Unacknowledged device-initiated notification.
- **Inform:** Acknowledged notification.
- **Syslog:** Timestamped event-message protocol.
- **DOM:** Digital Optical Monitoring—optical power, temperature, bias and related SFP measurements.

## Review questions

1. What is the difference between a MIB and an OID?  
2. Why should traps not replace polling?  
3. Which three evidence sources are most useful during an intermittent AV outage?

### Answers

1. A MIB defines the names and structure of available information; an OID identifies one particular value within that structure.  
2. Traps can be lost and provide events rather than continuous state or trends. Polling verifies current conditions and creates history.  
3. Time-aligned SNMP polling history, traps/syslog messages and the observed AV symptoms.

## Where we are headed

This lesson adds operational visibility to the networking foundation we have built. **Lesson 15 will cover certificates and PKI from the AV side:** why nearly every product says “this website is not trusted,” what the browser is actually objecting to, and how to correct it without teaching users to ignore security warnings.

title: Certificates and PKI: Why Every AV Web Interface Is “Not Trusted”
description: Understand browser trust warnings, certificate names, trust chains and practical AV certificate management.
markdown:
## Why an AV engineer should care

You enter a switch, DSP or control processor’s IP address. The login page appears, immediately accompanied by:

> Your connection is not private.

Often, the device is not actively attacking you. It shipped with a self-signed certificate that your computer has no reason to trust.

The warning still matters. If everyone learns to click through certificate errors automatically, nobody notices when a warning indicates an actual impersonation attempt. Today we’ll separate harmless-but-sloppy certificate problems from legitimate security problems—and fix the manageable ones.

### Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

- Explain what TLS certificates do—and what they do not do.
- Understand certificate authorities and trust chains.
- Diagnose common browser certificate warnings.
- Select a practical certificate strategy for an AV system.
- Define useful certificate requirements in BMT standards.

---

## 1. HTTPS is performing two related jobs

When you connect to:

`https://av-switch-01.client.com`

TLS attempts to provide:

1. **Encryption:** Someone observing the network should not be able to read the username, password or configuration data.
2. **Authentication:** Your browser should have reasonable evidence that it is talking to the real `av-switch-01.client.com`.

The server’s certificate contributes to authentication by binding an identity to a public key. The corresponding private key remains on the server. RFC 5280 describes certificates as structures that bind public keys to subjects through a trusted digital signature. ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280.html)) A certificate does **not** prove that:

- The product has no vulnerabilities.
- The web application is well written.
- The device’s administrator is trustworthy.
- The manufacturer still supports its firmware.
- The device belongs on the network.

It proves a narrower but valuable fact: a trusted issuer has associated the certificate’s stated identity with its public key, and the server can demonstrate possession of the matching private key.

---

## 2. The trust chain

Certificates normally form a chain:

- **Leaf certificate:** Installed on the switch, DSP or control processor.
- **Intermediate CA:** Signs leaf certificates.
- **Root CA:** The ultimate trust anchor.

Your computer maintains a **trust store** containing root CA certificates it already trusts. Public roots are generally supplied by Microsoft, Apple, Google, Mozilla or the operating-system vendor. A corporate IT department can also distribute its own private root to managed computers.

The browser validates the signatures upward:

`Device certificate → Intermediate CA → Trusted root CA`

If it can build and validate that chain, the issuer is trusted.

### What is a self-signed certificate?

A self-signed certificate signs itself. There is no independent CA above it.

That can still encrypt traffic. The problem is identity: anyone can make a self-signed certificate claiming to be your switch. Your browser cannot distinguish the legitimate certificate from an attacker’s homemade version.

This is why “encrypted” and “trusted” are not interchangeable.

Anyone can generate a certificate; other computers trust it only when its issuing root has been deliberately placed in their trust stores. ([letsencrypt.org](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/certificates-for-localhost/))

---

## 3. The browser performs several tests

A certificate must pass more than one test. The warning details usually identify which one failed.

| Browser complaint | What it usually means | Practical AV response |
|---|---|---|
| Issuer not trusted | Self-signed certificate or unknown private CA | Install a properly issued certificate or distribute the organization’s CA root |
| Name mismatch | Certificate covers a hostname, but you browsed by IP—or vice versa | Use the correct DNS name and include it in the certificate’s SAN |
| Expired certificate | Certificate passed its `Not After` date | Renew and replace it |
| Not valid yet | Device or computer clock may be wrong | Correct NTP, time zone and certificate dates |
| Incomplete chain | Device did not send an intermediate certificate | Import the complete certificate chain |
| Weak TLS or cipher error | Device firmware supports obsolete security | Update firmware; replacing only the certificate may not help |
| Certificate revoked | Issuer has invalidated the certificate | Replace it and investigate why it was revoked |

### The classic AV name mismatch

Suppose the certificate was issued for:

`av-core-01.customer.com`

But the technician opens:

`https://10.20.30.5`

The certificate may be completely legitimate, but it does not identify `10.20.30.5`. The browser requested one identity and received proof for another.

Modern certificates place valid names in the **Subject Alternative Name**, or **SAN**, extension. SAN entries can represent DNS names or IP addresses, but they must be encoded as the correct type. ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280.html)) A certificate containing:

`DNS:av-core-01.customer.com`

does not automatically cover:

- `10.20.30.5`
- `av-core-01`
- `av-switch-01.customer.com`
- Every other device on that VLAN

Use the exact hostname listed in the certificate. Although an IP address can be included as an IP SAN, stable DNS names are generally easier to manage.

---

## 4. Why accurate time suddenly matters again

Certificates contain a validity window:

- `Not Before`
- `Not After`

If a newly unboxed processor thinks it is January 1, 1970—or the year 2038—it may reject a valid certificate or present one that the browser considers invalid.

This gives NTP another AV job:

- Correct syslog timestamps
- Correct certificate validation
- Correct scheduled automation
- Better event correlation

BMT’s commissioning sequence should establish DNS, default gateway and NTP before testing secure web interfaces.

Otherwise, the certificate may be perfectly fine while the device is temporally living in the Nixon administration.

---

## 5. Three practical certificate strategies

### Strategy A: Manage a factory-certificate exception deliberately

Do not blindly bypass a browser warning. Any exception requires client IT approval and verification of the device identity and certificate fingerprint through a trusted, out-of-band source. Prefer correcting trust and hostname issues; this is not a routine click-through procedure.

For an isolated, temporary or very small system, replacing every certificate may create more work than value.

If the product only supports its factory self-signed certificate:

1. Connect from the intended management network.
2. Compare the certificate fingerprint with a known value when the manufacturer provides one.
3. Change default credentials immediately.
4. Record the limitation in closeout documentation.
5. Do not tell users that every certificate warning is harmless.

This is an acknowledged limitation, not a complete fix.

### Strategy B: Use the client’s internal CA

This is usually the best enterprise solution.

The client’s IT department issues certificates from an internal CA. Its root certificate is already trusted on managed workstations. Each AV device receives a unique certificate containing its assigned DNS name.

Example:

- Device IP: `10.40.12.21`
- DNS name: `av-qsys-01.campus.example.com`
- Certificate SAN: `DNS:av-qsys-01.campus.example.com`
- Issuer: Client Enterprise CA

This works well when:

- The client manages its computers.
- The AV management interfaces are private.
- The products support CSR generation or certificate import.
- IT owns certificate issuance and renewal.

### Strategy C: Use a publicly trusted CA

A public certificate can work when the organization owns a real domain and can validate control of it. A device does not necessarily need to be exposed to the internet; DNS-based validation can sometimes issue a certificate for an internally resolved hostname under a domain the client owns.

Example:

`av-switch-01.management.example.com`

This requires coordination, secure handling of private keys and a renewal process. Public CAs cannot simply certify arbitrary local names such as `switch01.local`; nobody uniquely owns those names. Let’s Encrypt makes the same point regarding `localhost` and recommends a locally trusted root for local-only certificates. ([letsencrypt.org](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/certificates-for-localhost/)) Do not expose an AV device’s web interface directly to the internet merely to obtain a certificate. That solves the wrong problem with impressive enthusiasm.

---

## 6. A practical installation workflow

Where the product supports custom certificates:

1. **Assign a stable management IP.**
2. **Create a DNS record** such as `av-dsp-01.site.customer.com`.
3. **Set DNS and NTP** on the device.
4. **Generate the private key and CSR on the device**, if possible.
5. Include the actual management hostname in the **SAN**.
6. Have the client’s CA or approved public CA sign the CSR.
7. Import the signed leaf certificate and any required intermediates.
8. Browse using the exact DNS name—not the raw IP.
9. Verify the certificate chain, hostname and expiration date.
10. Record the issuer, SAN, serial number, expiration and renewal owner.

A **CSR**, or Certificate Signing Request, contains the public key and requested identity information. It does not contain the private key.

Generating the key on the device is preferable because the private key never needs to leave it. If external generation is required, transfer it securely and delete working copies afterward.

Never install one shared certificate and private key on every AV product. If one box is compromised, every device using that key becomes impersonable.

---

## 7. Commercial-AV examples

### Example 1: Ruckus switch management

A technician opens `https://10.10.50.5` and receives a warning.

Inspection shows:

- The certificate is self-signed.
- Its name is unrelated to the project.
- It expired two years ago.
- HTTPS still encrypts the session, but identity validation fails.

For an enterprise project, BMT should request:

- DNS record: `av-sw-05.site.customer.com`
- Unique certificate containing that DNS SAN
- Issuance by the client’s trusted CA
- Certificate renewal assigned to IT or the service provider

The technician then uses the hostname shown on the drawings and equipment schedule.

### Example 2: DSP and control-processor interfaces

A Q-SYS Core, Biamp DSP or Crestron processor may offer HTTPS management, but certificate-management capabilities vary by model and firmware.

BMT should verify:

- Can it generate a CSR?
- Can it import a certificate and private key?
- Which formats does it accept: PEM, DER, PFX/P12?
- Can it store intermediate certificates?
- Does replacing firmware or performing a factory reset erase the certificate?
- Is there an API or management platform for renewal?

If custom certificates are unsupported, document the limitation rather than promising the client that every management page will become warning-free.

---

## BMT standards takeaway

Add a **Management Security** section to the device schedule containing:

- Management DNS name
- HTTPS support
- Custom certificate support
- Certificate issuer
- SAN entries
- Expiration date
- Renewal owner
- Certificate backup/recovery procedure
- Behavior after firmware update or factory reset

Also require that administrative drawings and closeout records use the DNS name where practical, not only the IP address.

## Practical exercise

Open the certificate details for one AV device that produces a browser warning. Record:

1. Issuer  
2. Subject and SAN entries  
3. Valid-from and expiration dates  
4. Hostname or IP used in the browser  
5. Whether the chain reaches a trusted root  

Then identify the exact failure:

- Unknown issuer?
- Name mismatch?
- Expired certificate?
- Incorrect clock?
- Missing intermediate?
- Obsolete TLS?

Do not install or trust anything during the exercise. Diagnose first.

## Compact glossary

- **TLS:** Protocol that secures the network session.
- **HTTPS:** HTTP carried inside TLS.
- **PKI:** Public Key Infrastructure—the certificates, authorities, policies and processes supporting trust.
- **CA:** Certificate Authority.
- **Root CA:** Highest trust anchor in a certificate chain.
- **Leaf certificate:** Certificate installed on the endpoint.
- **SAN:** Subject Alternative Name; lists identities covered by the certificate.
- **CSR:** Request submitted to a CA for certificate issuance.
- **Private key:** Secret key retained by the device.
- **Trust store:** Root certificates trusted by an operating system or application.

## Review questions

1. Can a self-signed certificate still encrypt traffic?  
2. Why does a valid certificate for `av-core-01.example.com` produce a warning when accessed through `10.20.30.5`?  
3. What must BMT document besides the certificate’s expiration date?

### Answers

1. Yes. It can provide encryption, but the browser cannot independently validate the server’s identity.  
2. The requested IP address does not match the certificate’s DNS identity.  
3. The issuer, SAN, renewal owner, replacement procedure and what happens after resets or firmware updates.

## Where we are headed

This completes our practical introduction to certificates and PKI. **Lesson 16 will cover secure remote AV support:** why direct port forwarding is dangerous, and how VPNs, jump hosts, vendor cloud services and zero-trust access can provide support without leaving a control processor hanging naked on the public internet. The requested USB 2/3, USB-C, PD and DisplayPort Alt Mode primer is also coming soon.

title: Secure Remote AV Support: Getting In Without Leaving the Door Open
description: Build a support path that reaches the right AV devices without exposing the whole network.
markdown:
## Why an AV engineer should care

Remote access is incredibly useful. It lets BMT troubleshoot a DSP, inspect switch counters or reload a control processor without flying across three states because someone claims “the TV thing is broken.”

It is also dangerous when implemented as:

> We forwarded port 443 through the firewall. Here’s the public IP and the admin password.

That exposes the AV product’s management interface directly to automated scanning, password attacks and any vulnerabilities hiding in its firmware. Today we’ll build safer paths that preserve remote support without placing an AV endpoint naked on the public internet.

### Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

- Explain what port forwarding exposes.
- Compare VPNs, jump hosts, vendor cloud services and zero-trust access.
- Design remote access around least privilege and MFA.
- Account for AV discovery tools that do not work across routed connections.
- Define BMT’s minimum remote-support requirements.

---

## 1. What happens during port forwarding

An internal device might have:

- Address: `10.20.30.40`
- HTTPS port: TCP 443

Private addresses are not normally reachable from the internet. The firewall uses NAT to translate between the internal network and its public address.

A port-forwarding rule might say:

> Any connection arriving at public TCP port 8443 should be forwarded to `10.20.30.40:443`.

That effectively publishes the AV device’s login page to the world.

Changing external port 443 to something unusual like 48,327 does not provide meaningful security. Internet scanners examine every port. A weird port may reduce casual noise, but it does not make the service private.

HTTPS also does not solve this problem. HTTPS encrypts the session; it does not compensate for:

- Default credentials
- Weak passwords
- Unpatched firmware
- Authentication bypass vulnerabilities
- Obsolete TLS libraries
- Unlimited login attempts
- Missing MFA
- Poor event logging

CISA recommends removing unnecessary management interfaces from internet exposure or placing a separate zero-trust policy-enforcement point in front of them. The principle applies directly to AV equipment, even though the federal directive that prompted it specifically governs federal agencies. ([cisa.gov](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2023/06/13/cisa-issues-bod-23-02-mitigating-risk-internet-exposed-management-interfaces))

---

## 2. The correct question is not “Can I reach it?”

The correct question is:

> Who can reach exactly which resource, after proving what, and where is that access recorded?

Good remote access should establish:

1. **Identity:** Who is connecting?
2. **Authentication:** How did they prove it?
3. **Authorization:** What may they access?
4. **Device condition:** Are they connecting from an approved, secured computer?
5. **Time:** Is the access permanent or temporary?
6. **Evidence:** Are login and administrative events recorded?
7. **Revocation:** How quickly can access be removed?

This is the useful part of **zero trust**. It does not mean trusting absolutely nobody and requiring seventeen passwords to adjust a fader.

It means that being “inside the network” does not automatically earn unlimited access. NIST’s Zero Trust Architecture says trust should not be granted solely because a user or device is on the LAN; authentication and authorization occur before access to a resource is established. ([csrc.nist.gov](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/207/final))

---

## 3. Five remote-access approaches

### A. Direct port forwarding

**Internet → Firewall rule → AV device**

This is the weakest normal approach.

The AV product itself must withstand every internet attack, yet AV devices often have long firmware lifecycles, limited logging and no MFA.

**BMT position:** Do not specify or establish direct forwarding to switch, DSP, control, signage or AVoIP management interfaces.

An IP allowlist can reduce exposure when an emergency exception is unavoidable, but it is still an exception—not the preferred architecture.

### B. Client VPN

**Technician → VPN gateway → Client network → AV device**

The VPN authenticates the technician and establishes an encrypted tunnel into the site.

Advantages:

- AV endpoints remain private.
- Access can use MFA.
- The client controls authorization.
- One gateway can protect many internal devices.

Weaknesses:

- A poorly configured VPN may provide access to the entire corporate network.
- A compromised technician laptop can become an entry point.
- Some AV discovery applications do not work across routed VPN connections.
- The VPN gateway itself becomes important security infrastructure and must be maintained.

The VPN should permit BMT access only to the required AV management subnet, ports and services—not “any to any because we were troubleshooting and got impatient.”

### C. VPN plus jump host

**Technician → VPN/MFA → On-site jump host → AV management VLAN**

A **jump host**, also called a bastion host, is a controlled computer used for administration. BMT remotely operates that computer, and the computer communicates with the AV equipment locally.

This is often the most practical enterprise AV approach because software such as Dante Controller, Crestron Toolbox, Q-SYS Designer or manufacturer discovery utilities may expect local broadcast, multicast or Layer 2 behavior.

The remote technician’s laptop does not need to participate directly in those discovery protocols. The on-site jump host does.

A good jump host should have:

- Current operating-system and application patches
- Endpoint protection
- MFA at the remote-access layer
- Named user accounts
- Limited access to the AV management network
- Session and login logging
- No casual web browsing or email
- Approved AV service applications only
- Configuration files stored in a controlled location

Do not use the front-desk computer as the permanent AV jump host. Donna clicking a coupon attachment should not become part of the signal path.

### D. Vendor cloud platform

**AV device or agent → Outbound encrypted connection → Vendor cloud ← Technician**

Many platforms establish an outbound connection to a cloud service. Because the session originates inside the site, no inbound firewall port may be required.

This can be a good solution, but “cloud” is not automatically synonymous with “secure.”

Evaluate:

- Does it support MFA?
- Are accounts individual or shared?
- Can access be divided by customer and site?
- Are administrative actions logged?
- Can BMT’s access be revoked without affecting the client?
- What device data leaves the site?
- Does the product continue operating during a cloud outage?
- Is the cloud connection required for operation or only management?
- What happens when the subscription expires?
- How quickly does the vendor address vulnerabilities?

Cloud management should fail safely. A lost internet connection must not make the conference room forget how to conference.

### E. Zero-trust or application-specific access

**Technician → Identity and policy check → Approved resource**

A zero-trust access broker can expose a particular application or management service without granting the user general network access.

For example, a technician may receive HTTPS access to:

`av-monitor.customer.com`

but no direct reachability to the client’s user, finance or server networks.

This is cleaner than a broad VPN when the required management functions work through normal routed applications. It may be less useful for tools needing broadcast discovery, in which case a jump host remains appropriate.

---

## 4. Why AV discovery complicates remote support

Many AV programs locate devices using:

- Layer 2 broadcasts
- Multicast discovery
- mDNS
- Vendor-specific discovery packets

Routers normally do not forward broadcasts. VPNs and zero-trust connections are commonly routed rather than bridged.

Therefore, the technician may be able to ping a processor by IP but still see an empty discovery window.

The safe solutions are usually:

1. Connect to devices directly by known IP or DNS name.
2. Run the manufacturer’s tool on an on-site jump host.
3. Use an approved discovery gateway where the protocol supports one.
4. Use the manufacturer’s management platform or directory service.

Avoid stretching Layer 2 across the internet simply to make a discovery button work. Extending a VLAN remotely creates a much larger failure and security domain for very little practical benefit.

Good documentation solves part of this problem. If BMT’s closeout package contains accurate addresses, DNS names, VLANs and credentials handling instructions, discovery becomes convenient rather than essential.

---

## 5. Commercial-AV examples

### Example 1: Enterprise control and audio system

A client has:

- Ruckus ICX switches
- Q-SYS Cores
- Crestron processors
- Dante devices
- Separate AV management and Dante VLANs

BMT receives a named VPN account protected by MFA. The firewall permits that account to reach one hardened jump host.

The jump host can reach:

- HTTPS and SSH on the AV switches
- Q-SYS management addresses
- Crestron processors
- Dante devices through its approved local interface

It cannot reach:

- Employee computers
- Accounting servers
- Building access-control systems
- The client’s general server VLAN

Dante Controller runs on the jump host because Dante discovery and clocking traffic should remain local. Remote desktop carries the screen and user input—not the Dante network itself.

### Example 2: Multi-location signage and sports-bar AV

A venue group has BrightSign players, managed displays and AVoIP endpoints at several locations.

The bad design forwards a unique public port to every player and decoder. The resulting spreadsheet becomes a directory of publicly reachable equipment.

The better design uses:

- Vendor cloud management for supported signage functions
- A VPN or outbound remote-support appliance for local equipment
- Per-site access permissions
- MFA
- Centralized logs
- No inbound forwarding to individual AV endpoints

If BMT’s contract ends, its accounts can be removed centrally without changing the local operation of every display.

---

## 6. BMT’s remote-support baseline

Remote access should require:

- No direct internet exposure of AV management interfaces
- MFA for all remote users
- Named accounts—no shared `bmtadmin` account
- Least-privilege access to required VLANs, devices and ports
- A client-approved VPN, jump host, zero-trust gateway or cloud platform
- Logs showing successful and failed access
- Immediate revocation for former staff and vendors
- Defined patch responsibility for the remote-access gateway and jump host
- Secure credential storage
- Configuration backup before significant remote changes
- Local AV operation independent of the remote-access service
- Remote access documented on the network diagram and closeout package

CISA’s current exposure-reduction guidance similarly recommends removing unnecessary exposure, using jump hosts, maintaining patches, monitoring traffic and applying MFA. ([cisa.gov](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/exposure-reduction)) Remote desktop and RMM tools are legitimate but powerful. Threat actors use the same tools because they provide real administrative control. CISA recommends controlling which remote-access products are permitted, applying segmentation and recording their use. ([cisa.gov](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/guide-securing-remote-access-software?idU=1&utm_source=chatgpt.com))

---

## Practical exercise

Choose one existing BMT-supported site and complete this path:

`Internet → ______ → ______ → AV management VLAN → Device`

Then answer:

1. Where does authentication occur?
2. Is MFA required?
3. Does the technician receive the whole network or only AV resources?
4. Where are login attempts recorded?
5. Can the client revoke BMT without reconfiguring every AV device?
6. Does the AV system keep operating if remote access fails?

If the completed path is merely:

`Internet → Port forward → Control processor`

you have found the improvement project.

## Compact glossary

- **NAT:** Translation between internal and external addresses.
- **Port forwarding:** Maps an inbound public port to an internal service.
- **VPN:** Encrypted connection into a private network.
- **MFA:** Authentication using more than one factor.
- **Jump host:** Controlled computer used to administer other devices.
- **Bastion host:** Another name for a hardened jump host.
- **RMM:** Remote Monitoring and Management software.
- **Zero trust:** Resource access based on verified identity and policy, not assumed trust from network location.
- **Least privilege:** Grant only the access required for the task.
- **Allowlist:** Explicit list of approved users, addresses, applications or services.

## Review questions

1. Why is moving a forwarded web interface to an unusual port not real security?  
2. Why might Dante Controller work on an on-site jump host but not directly across a VPN?  
3. What is the central idea behind zero trust?

### Answers

1. Internet scanners inspect all ports, and the underlying device remains publicly reachable and attackable.  
2. Dante discovery relies heavily on local multicast and Layer 2 behavior that a routed VPN generally does not carry.  
3. Access is granted to specific resources after verifying identity and policy; being inside the LAN does not automatically make someone trusted.

## Where we are headed

This lesson connects networking, identity, certificates and logging into a practical support architecture. **Lesson 17 will cover AV vulnerability and firmware management:** CVEs, support lifecycles, patch decisions, configuration backups and how to update equipment without turning a functioning venue into an involuntary test lab.

title: Firmware, CVEs and Vulnerability Management for AV
description: Prioritize vulnerabilities, stage firmware updates and verify the room still works after maintenance.
markdown:
## Why an AV engineer should care

AV systems live in an awkward place: they are networked computers expected to behave like permanently installed appliances.

IT may want every security update installed immediately. Operations may want nothing touched because the system currently works. Both positions make sense—and both become dangerous when treated as absolutes.

The goal is not “always update” or “never update.” It is:

> Understand the exposure, prioritize the risk, preserve a rollback path, and verify the AV system afterward.

### Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

- Distinguish a CVE identifier from a CVSS score and confirmed exploitation.
- Prioritize AV vulnerabilities using exposure and operational impact.
- Prepare an AV system for a safe firmware update.
- Validate networked AV functions after an update.
- Define useful vulnerability-management requirements for BMT projects.

---

## 1. Firmware is software wearing work boots

A switch, DSP, encoder or control processor contains software even when the manufacturer calls it firmware.

That may include:

- Operating system
- Web server
- SSH server
- Network protocol stacks
- Device-management services
- Media-processing code
- Control application
- Bootloader
- Third-party software libraries

A vulnerability in one bundled library can affect many products. The AV manufacturer may not have written the vulnerable component, but it still must provide an updated product image containing the fix.

### Update terminology

Manufacturers use these terms inconsistently, but generally:

- **Patch:** Narrow fix for a specific problem.
- **Maintenance release:** Collection of bug and security fixes.
- **Feature release:** Adds capabilities and may change behavior.
- **Firmware upgrade:** Replaces much of the device’s operating software.
- **Bootloader update:** Changes the low-level software that starts the device.
- **Hotfix:** Targeted fix released outside the normal schedule.

Do not assume “firmware 10” is simply “firmware 9, but safer.” A major release may introduce different configuration behavior, file formats or companion-software requirements.

---

## 2. CVE, CVSS and KEV are three different things

### CVE: the identification number

A **CVE**, or Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures identifier, gives a publicly disclosed vulnerability a unique name.

Example:

`CVE-YYYY-NNNNN` (illustrative format, not a cited vulnerability)

The number does not tell you whether the vulnerability is severe or whether it affects your exact product configuration. It gives manufacturers, researchers and customers a common reference.

Think of CVE as the case number.

### CVSS: estimated technical severity

The **Common Vulnerability Scoring System** produces a severity score, normally from 0.0 to 10.0.

It considers technical characteristics such as:

- Whether the attack can be performed remotely
- Whether authentication is required
- Attack complexity
- User interaction
- Effect on confidentiality, integrity and availability

A score of 9.8 gets attention, but it does not automatically mean “patch every affected device tonight.”

NIST explicitly states that CVSS measures **severity**, not organizational risk. ([nvd.nist.gov](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln-metrics/cvss)) Risk also depends on:

- Is the service enabled?
- Is the device reachable from the internet?
- Can normal users reach its management interface?
- Is there a working exploit?
- What could an attacker control?
- What happens if the update breaks the AV system?
- Are compensating controls already reducing exposure?

### KEV: confirmed exploitation

CISA’s **Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog** contains vulnerabilities for which there is evidence of real-world exploitation.

That is a major priority signal. A theoretically severe vulnerability and a vulnerability attackers are actively using are not the same operational situation. CISA recommends using the KEV catalog as an input to vulnerability prioritization. ([cisa.gov](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog)) A useful mental model is:

- **CVE:** Which vulnerability?
- **CVSS:** How technically severe could it be?
- **KEV:** Are attackers actually exploiting it?
- **Your architecture:** Can they reach it, and what could they damage?

---

## 3. Prioritizing an AV vulnerability

Use four questions.

### 1. Is the affected feature present and enabled?

A bulletin might concern:

- Web management
- SSH
- Bluetooth
- USB file import
- Vendor cloud connection
- A discovery protocol
- A specific software library

If the affected service is disabled, the device may still technically contain the vulnerable code, but immediate exposure is lower.

### 2. Who can reach the device?

Exposure increases roughly in this order:

1. Directly reachable from the internet
2. Reachable through a vendor cloud or remote-access system
3. Reachable from the general corporate network
4. Reachable only from a restricted AV management VLAN
5. Physically isolated with no active network connection

Segmentation does not erase a vulnerability. It can provide time to test and schedule remediation safely.

### 3. What can exploitation accomplish?

Possible outcomes include:

- Read configuration information
- Steal credentials
- Change settings
- Execute arbitrary code
- Interrupt audio or video
- Move laterally into other networks
- Permanently damage configuration
- Use the AV device as a launching point

A denial-of-service vulnerability on a lobby signage player and remote code execution on the core switch are not equal business risks, even if their numerical scores appear similar.

### 4. What is the update risk?

Consider:

- Is the release recommended by the manufacturer?
- Is it a stable maintenance release or a new feature train?
- Does it require intermediate upgrade steps?
- Does it change configuration syntax?
- Does it require a new version of the programming software?
- Can the previous image and configuration be restored?
- Is console access available if networking fails?
- Has the update been tested on equivalent hardware?

This produces a practical priority:

| Condition | BMT response |
|---|---|
| Internet-exposed, actively exploited or remotely exploitable | Remove exposure immediately; patch urgently after controlled preparation |
| Reachable from broad client networks with serious impact | Apply temporary restrictions and schedule prompt remediation |
| Isolated management network with compensating controls | Test first, then install during a planned window |
| Low-impact feature disabled and no known exploitation | Track and include in routine maintenance |
| Product no longer receives security updates | Restrict aggressively and plan replacement |

---

## 4. The AV-safe update workflow

NIST defines patch management as identifying, prioritizing, acquiring, installing and verifying updates. It treats patching as preventive maintenance—not a random late-night adventure. ([csrc.nist.gov](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/40/r4/final)) For AV, use the following workflow.

### Step 1: Inventory

Record:

- Manufacturer and model
- Serial number
- Current firmware and bootloader
- Companion-software version
- Configuration or project-file version
- IP address and hostname
- Support and warranty status
- Installed options or licenses
- Known dependencies

SNMP may automatically collect some firmware and inventory information, depending on what the product exposes.

### Step 2: Read the release notes

Look for:

- Security fixes
- Known problems
- Required upgrade path
- Hardware-revision limitations
- Configuration conversion
- Downgrade restrictions
- Companion-software requirements
- Factory-reset warnings
- Cluster, stack or redundant-system procedure

“New firmware available” is not sufficient engineering information.

### Step 3: Capture the known-good state

Before touching the device:

- Export its configuration.
- Save the programming source file.
- Record current firmware.
- Back up certificates where supported.
- Capture licenses and activation information.
- Save switch running and startup configurations.
- Photograph or export important status pages.
- Confirm access to the old firmware image.
- Confirm the recovery or console procedure.

A backup is not a rollback plan unless you know how to restore it.

### Step 4: Test or stage

Where possible:

- Test on spare or equivalent hardware.
- Load a copied configuration.
- Confirm device discovery and control.
- Verify interoperability with surrounding equipment.
- Let it run long enough to reveal obvious stability issues.

Smaller projects may not have spare hardware. In that case, increase preparation, schedule on-site support and avoid updating immediately before an important event.

### Step 5: Establish the maintenance window

Define:

- Systems affected
- Expected outage
- Responsible technician
- Client approval
- Recovery threshold
- Rollback decision time
- On-site or remote coverage
- Post-update test list

Do not update the sports bar’s video core two hours before Sunday kickoff because the release notes used the word “recommended.”

### Step 6: Install in the documented order

The correct order varies.

A manufacturer might require:

- Management server before endpoints
- Controller before peripherals
- Stack members in a specific sequence
- Intermediate firmware before the current release
- Application software upgraded before opening the project

Follow the product-specific procedure. There is no universal “always update the core first” rule.

### Step 7: Validate the entire AV workflow

A green power LED is not acceptance testing.

Confirm:

- Device boots and retains its configuration
- Management login and certificates work
- Control interfaces operate
- Audio passes correctly
- Video routes and HDCP function
- USB extension works where used
- Dante or AES67 subscriptions recover
- PTP clock status is stable
- Multicast receivers join and leave correctly
- IGMP querier and snooping remain correct
- VLANs and trunks are unchanged
- PoE endpoints power correctly
- SNMP polling and syslog resume
- Remote access still works
- Redundancy or failover operates where applicable

Then record the new version and archive the post-update configuration.

---

## 5. Commercial-AV examples

### Example 1: Ruckus ICX switch carrying AVoIP

A new FastIron release includes security fixes. The switch is also carrying multicast video and PoE endpoints.

Before updating, BMT should capture:

- Running and startup configuration
- Boot preference and both firmware-image slots
- VLANs and tagged/untagged port assignments
- IGMP snooping and querier configuration
- Spanning-tree state
- PoE status
- SFP DOM readings
- Port error and discard counters
- LLDP neighbors

Afterward, test multicast routing and receiver changes—not merely internet connectivity. Also confirm that the switch booted the intended image. Loading firmware into secondary flash is not useful if the boot command quietly returns to the old version.

### Example 2: Q-SYS, Crestron or Biamp platform update

A processor update may require a matching designer or programming-software version.

Before upgrading:

- Preserve the editable source project.
- Confirm that the new software can open and deploy it.
- Identify plugins, scripts or modules that may be incompatible.
- Verify that a converted project can be downgraded—or save an untouched copy.
- Confirm touchpanels, peripherals and control modules support the target release.

A processor that boots successfully but no longer communicates with a third-party display is not a successful update.

---

## BMT standards takeaway

Add a **Software and Support Register** to project closeout records:

- Product and model
- Installed firmware
- Configuration-tool version
- Latest tested BMT version
- Vendor support status
- Security-advisory URL
- Configuration-backup location
- Upgrade and recovery procedure
- Last review date
- Responsible party
- Known dependencies

Specifications should also require manufacturers to disclose:

- Security-support period
- Vulnerability-reporting contact
- Firmware-update process
- Whether configurations survive updates
- Whether downgrade is supported
- End-of-support notification policy

## Practical exercise

Choose one active AV product and find its current firmware and release notes.

Without installing anything, write down:

1. Current installed version  
2. Available target version  
3. Security issues fixed  
4. Required intermediate versions  
5. Configuration backup method  
6. Rollback method  
7. Companion-software requirement  
8. Five post-update tests  

Then decide: urgent, prompt, routine or defer with compensating controls.

The point is to make a defensible decision—not reflexively click **Update All** and hope the building respects your confidence.

## Compact glossary

- **CVE:** Unique identifier for a publicly disclosed vulnerability.
- **CVSS:** Technical-severity scoring system; not a complete risk score.
- **KEV:** CISA catalog of vulnerabilities with known exploitation.
- **Firmware:** Software embedded in a device.
- **Exploit:** Technique or code that takes advantage of a vulnerability.
- **Compensating control:** Protection that reduces risk without removing the underlying vulnerability.
- **EOL:** End of Life.
- **EOS:** End of Support or End of Sale, depending on the manufacturer.
- **Rollback:** Restoring the previous software and configuration.
- **Maintenance window:** Approved period for potentially disruptive work.

## Review questions

1. Why should BMT not prioritize vulnerabilities using CVSS alone?  
2. What is the difference between a configuration backup and a rollback plan?  
3. What does presence in CISA’s KEV catalog tell you?

### Answers

1. CVSS estimates technical severity but does not include BMT’s exposure, architecture, operational impact or compensating controls.  
2. A backup is stored data; a rollback plan includes the previous image, restoration procedure, access method, decision point and validation steps.  
3. There is evidence that attackers have exploited the vulnerability in real-world conditions, making remediation a higher priority.

## Where we are headed

We have now completed the first networking and security foundation. **Lesson 18 will be the requested practical USB primer:** USB 2.0 versus USB 3.x, cameras, conferencing, USB-C, Power Delivery, DisplayPort Alt Mode, extension limits and why USB over AVoIP can become a bandwidth and topology problem.

title: USB for AV: Data, Cameras, Extension, USB-C, PD and DP Alt Mode
description: Understand USB hosts, bandwidth, extension, USB-C, Power Delivery and DisplayPort Alt Mode.
markdown:
## Why an AV engineer should care

USB causes trouble because one familiar connector can carry several unrelated things:

- Peripheral data
- DisplayPort video
- Charging power
- Sometimes Thunderbolt or USB4 traffic

A USB-C connector guarantees only the connector shape. It does **not** guarantee USB 3 data, video output, laptop charging or Thunderbolt.

For AV, the essential question is therefore not “Does it have USB-C?” It is:

> What functions do the host, cable, extender and endpoint mutually support?

### Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

- Choose between USB 2.0, USB 3.x and USB4 for common AV devices.
- Explain USB host/device relationships and enumeration.
- Estimate whether a camera can operate within USB 2.0 bandwidth.
- Distinguish USB-C, USB Power Delivery and DisplayPort Alt Mode.
- Select an appropriate USB-extension method.

---

## 1. USB begins with a host

USB is **host-centric**. The host—usually a computer—controls the connection.

When you attach a camera, microphone or DSP:

1. The host detects an electrical connection.
2. It resets and addresses the device.
3. The device identifies itself.
4. The host loads an appropriate driver.
5. The host requests the device’s available functions and bandwidth.
6. Data transfer begins.

This identification process is called **enumeration**.

That matters because USB is not Ethernet. A USB camera does not independently send packets wherever it chooses. It expects to be attached to one USB host, either directly or through infrastructure that convincingly extends that relationship.

A USB hub simply gives one host additional peripheral connections. It is not a network switch and does not route devices among multiple computers.

If several computers must share one camera, something must actively change the host relationship:

- USB switcher
- Matrix switcher with USB routing
- KVM system
- USB-over-IP system
- Conferencing appliance acting as an intermediary

---

## 2. USB generations and actual AV use

| Technology | Signaling rate | Typical AV uses |
|---|---:|---|
| USB 2.0 High-Speed | 480 Mb/s | Audio interfaces, DSPs, control, HID and compressed cameras |
| USB 3.2 Gen 1 | 5 Gb/s | Higher-resolution cameras, capture devices and storage |
| USB 3.2 Gen 2 | 10 Gb/s | High-performance capture and storage |
| USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 | 20 Gb/s | Specialized storage; relatively uncommon in installed AV |
| USB4 | 20, 40 or 80 Gb/s | Docks and high-performance data/display systems |

USB-IF’s current USB 3.2 terminology defines 5, 10 and 20 Gb/s operating rates. USB4 now extends as high as 80 Gb/s. ([usb.org](https://www.usb.org/usb-32-0), [usb.org](https://www.usb.org/usb4)) These are raw signaling rates, not guaranteed application throughput. Protocol overhead, hubs, host controllers, drivers and competing devices reduce usable bandwidth.

### Why some 1080p cameras need USB 3

An uncompressed 1080p30 video stream using 16 bits per pixel requires approximately:


```text
1920 × 1080 × 30 × 16 ≈ 995 Mb/s
```


That cannot fit through USB 2.0’s 480 Mb/s signaling rate.

Yet many 1080p cameras work perfectly over USB 2.0 because they send compressed MJPEG or H.264 rather than uncompressed pixels. Compression reduces bandwidth but may add latency, image artifacts and processing requirements.

A USB 3 camera may need SuperSpeed because it provides:

- Uncompressed or lightly compressed video
- 4K resolution
- Higher frame rates
- Multiple simultaneous video streams
- Additional audio or sensor data

Therefore, “1080p camera” is not enough information. BMT should record the required resolution, frame rate, pixel format or codec, and required USB generation.

---

## 3. Transfer types explain extender compatibility

USB supports different transfer behaviors:

- **Control:** Setup, enumeration and configuration.
- **Interrupt:** Small, responsive transactions such as keyboards and touchscreens.
- **Bulk:** Large transfers whose timing can vary, such as files and some video devices.
- **Isochronous:** Time-sensitive streams such as audio and many cameras; timely delivery matters more than retransmitting every error.

An extender described only as “USB compatible” may support keyboards and mice while failing with a camera or audio interface.

For any USB extender, confirm:

- USB generation and speed
- Isochronous support
- UVC camera support
- UAC audio support
- Number and type of hubs allowed
- Available current at the remote end
- Whether firmware or drivers are required
- Tested operating systems and devices

**HID support is not equivalent to general USB 2.0 support.**

---

## 4. USB-C is only the connector

A USB-C port could support:

- USB 2.0 only
- USB 3.2
- USB4
- Charging only
- Power Delivery
- DisplayPort Alt Mode
- Thunderbolt
- Some combination of these

USB-IF explicitly distinguishes USB Type-C from USB 3.2 and USB4. A USB-C cable can legitimately carry only USB 2.0 data, even if it supports substantial charging power. ([usb.org](https://www.usb.org/sites/default/files/usb_type-c_language_product_and_packaging_guidelines_20230320.pdf)) When specifying a USB-C connection, document its functions separately:

| Function | Requirement example |
|---|---|
| Connector | USB Type-C |
| Data | USB 3.2, 5 Gb/s |
| Video | DisplayPort Alt Mode |
| Power | 90 W USB PD to laptop |
| Peripheral role | Laptop is USB host |
| Cable | Certified for required data and power |

Never treat the phrase “full-featured USB-C” as a sufficiently precise specification.

---

## 5. USB Power Delivery

Basic USB can provide power without USB PD, but only within the applicable port’s normal power rules. **USB Power Delivery** adds communication between the power source and power-consuming device.

A typical negotiation is:

1. The charger or dock advertises available power profiles.
2. The laptop requests one it supports.
3. They agree on voltage and current.
4. Higher power is enabled only after negotiation.

USB PD Revision 3.1 expanded the maximum from 100 W to 240 W when the devices and cable support the required Extended Power Range capability. ([usb.org](https://www.usb.org/usb-charger-pd)) Practical traps include:

- A 100 W power supply does not mean the laptop receives 100 W; the dock consumes some.
- A cable may support 240 W power but only USB 2.0 data.
- Higher-current cables require electronic identification.
- The laptop, dock, power supply and cable negotiate to their **lowest mutual capability**.
- A powerful workstation may operate but slowly discharge if the dock supplies less power than it consumes.

For BMT drawings, label laptop connections with the **minimum delivered wattage at the user port**, not merely the power-supply rating.

---

## 6. DisplayPort Alt Mode

**DisplayPort Alternate Mode** lets a USB-C connector assign some of its high-speed conductors to native DisplayPort video. VESA describes it as carrying DisplayPort alongside USB data and power through USB-C. ([vesa.org](https://vesa.org/featured-articles/vesa-releases-updated-displayport-alt-mode-spec-to-bring-displayport-2-0-performance-to-usb4-and-new-usb-type-c-devices/)) A single conference-room cable can therefore provide:

- Video from the laptop to the display system
- USB data between the laptop and room camera/DSP
- Charging power back to the laptop

However, using high-speed lanes for DisplayPort can reduce the lanes available for USB 3 data. Some implementations provide high-resolution video plus only USB 2.0 peripheral data. Others divide the lanes between DisplayPort and SuperSpeed USB.

This explains a classic failure:

> The laptop charges and the display works, but the USB 3 camera connects at USB 2 speed—or does not work at the requested format.

The connector fits. The lane allocation does not.

---

## 7. Extending USB in real rooms

Passive copper works well across a desk, not necessarily from a credenza to a camera above an 86-inch display.

Useful planning categories are:

1. **Passive cable:** Simplest and most reliable for short distances. As a conservative design heuristic, keep USB 2 near 5 metres and SuperSpeed USB around 2–3 metres unless the certified cable manufacturer states otherwise.

2. **Active repeater cable:** Regenerates the signal. Confirm power, maximum chained sections and camera compatibility.

3. **Active optical USB cable:** Useful across tens of metres. Often directional; some do not carry useful remote power or support every USB-C function.

4. **Point-to-point extender:** Local and remote boxes connected by category cable or fiber. Good products explicitly support USB 2 or USB 3, hubs and isochronous devices.

5. **USB over IP or AVoIP:** Encapsulates USB across a network or proprietary packet fabric. Useful for routing but dependent on the product’s supported USB classes, latency and bandwidth.

Do not assume a category-cable extender is normal Ethernet. Many use Cat cable as convenient transport but cannot pass through a network switch.

---

## 8. Commercial-AV examples

### Example 1: BYOD conferencing room

A laptop connects through one USB-C cable to a dock. The dock provides:

- DisplayPort Alt Mode video
- USB connection to a Q-SYS, Biamp or similar conferencing audio interface
- USB connection to the room camera
- Laptop charging

The audio interface may require little bandwidth. The camera may be the deciding factor. If the dock exposes only USB 2 after allocating lanes to video, the camera must offer a suitable compressed USB 2 mode.

BMT should test the complete chain with representative Windows and macOS laptops—not merely confirm each component separately.

### Example 2: USB through an AVoIP/KVM system

A Crestron NVX or comparable system may route USB for keyboard/mouse control or other supported peripherals, depending on the exact endpoint model and configuration.

Before promising camera transport, verify whether the system supports:

- General USB or HID only
- UVC and UAC classes
- Isochronous transfers
- Required USB speed
- Simultaneous users
- Host switching behavior

A compressed USB camera could consume hundreds of megabits per second. An uncompressed USB 3 camera can exceed a 1 Gb/s network path. USB must therefore appear in the bandwidth and topology calculations—it is not free just because the video is already “on the network.”

---

## BMT design takeaway

Add a **USB Connection Schedule** containing:

- Host and peripheral
- Connector type
- Required USB speed
- Device class: HID, UVC, UAC or other
- Maximum bandwidth or tested format
- Power required at the endpoint
- Extension technology and distance
- Directionality
- Host-switching requirement
- Approved cable/extender model
- Tested firmware and operating systems

## Practical exercise

Inspect one USB-C conferencing connection and answer:

1. Which device is the USB host?
2. Is the camera operating at USB 2 or USB 3?
3. What video format is it sending?
4. Does the connection carry DisplayPort?
5. How much power reaches the laptop?
6. What would stop working if the cable supported only USB 2?

## Compact glossary

- **Host:** Computer controlling the USB bus.
- **Enumeration:** Host’s process of detecting and configuring a device.
- **HID:** Human Interface Device.
- **UVC:** USB Video Class.
- **UAC:** USB Audio Class.
- **PD:** Power Delivery.
- **DP Alt Mode:** DisplayPort signals carried through USB-C.
- **Isochronous:** Time-sensitive USB transfer type.
- **E-marker:** Chip identifying a USB-C cable’s capabilities.

## Review questions

1. Why can a 1080p camera work over USB 2 while another requires USB 3?  
2. Does USB-C guarantee DisplayPort video and laptop charging?  
3. Why might a USB extender work with a keyboard but fail with a camera?

### Answers

1. One may send compressed video, while the other sends uncompressed video, higher frame rates or multiple streams.  
2. No. Connector shape, data speed, Alt Mode and PD capability are separate properties.  
3. Keyboard traffic is low-bandwidth interrupt traffic; the camera may require high bandwidth, isochronous support and compatible UVC handling.

## Where we are headed

This requested USB primer bridges AV hardware and network transport. **Lesson 19 will move into AV-over-IP architecture:** what is actually being packetized, unicast versus multicast distribution, control versus media planes, bandwidth domains and how to read an AVoIP topology without accepting the manufacturer’s cloud-shaped box as an explanation.

title: AV-over-IP Architecture: What Is Actually Moving?
description: Map media, control, discovery and timing flows to a network that can actually carry them.
markdown:
## Why an AV engineer should care

An AVoIP drawing often shows encoders, decoders and a cloud labeled **NETWORK**. That is approximately as useful as labeling an electrical riser **ELECTRICITY HAPPENS HERE**.

To design or troubleshoot the system, you need to know:

- What traffic each endpoint generates
- Whether it is unicast or multicast
- Which links carry each stream
- What is media versus control or management
- Where bandwidth can become oversubscribed
- What happens after a link or switch fails

### Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

- Describe how an AV signal becomes network traffic.
- Distinguish unicast from multicast distribution.
- Separate media, control, management and timing functions.
- Calculate bandwidth at endpoint and uplink levels.
- Read an AVoIP topology as a set of traffic paths rather than a collection of boxes.

---

## 1. From HDMI to Ethernet—and back

A basic AVoIP path looks like this:

1. A source produces HDMI, SDI, audio or another baseband signal.
2. An encoder captures the signal.
3. It may compress the audio or video.
4. It divides the resulting data into small payloads.
5. Protocol headers are added.
6. The endpoint transmits Ethernet frames through the network.
7. A decoder receives the packets.
8. It buffers, reorders and possibly decompresses them.
9. It reconstructs an HDMI, SDI, audio or USB output.

The switch does not understand that the packets contain a football game, camera image or Dante channel. It principally acts on Ethernet and IP information:

- Source and destination MAC addresses
- VLAN tag
- Source and destination IP addresses
- Multicast group
- QoS markings
- Transport protocol and port, when relevant to features such as ACLs

The encoder and decoder understand the media. The network moves packets according to addressing and policy.

### “Stream” and “flow”

Manufacturers use these words inconsistently.

For our purposes:

- A **stream** is one logical media transmission, such as an encoded video source.
- A **flow** is a particular packet transmission from a sender, potentially containing one or more channels.

Dante, for example, can place multiple audio channels into one network flow. Other platforms may treat every video source as its own stream and multicast group.

Always check the manufacturer’s definition before calculating a system from the word alone.

---

## 2. Compression determines the network

An encoder does not automatically make video small. Its codec and operating mode determine the data rate.

### Uncompressed

Uncompressed video preserves the original samples without a compression process. Quality and latency can be excellent, but the bandwidth is substantial.

A rough active-pixel calculation for 1080p60, 10-bit, 4:2:2 video is:


```text
1920 × 1080 × 60 × 20 ≈ 2.49 Gb/s
```


Packet headers and other transport requirements increase the carried rate. Uncompressed 4K60 is roughly four times that pixel payload.

This is why uncompressed professional-video systems commonly require 10, 25 or faster Ethernet.

SMPTE ST 2110 can transport video, audio and ancillary data as separate, accurately timed streams. ST 2110-20 defines uncompressed video, while ST 2110-30 covers PCM audio by reference to AES67. ([smpte.org](https://www.smpte.org/standards/ST2110))

### Light or visually lossless compression

JPEG XS, JPEG 2000 and proprietary low-latency codecs can reduce video sufficiently for 1 or 10 Gb/s networks while preserving high image quality.

Depending on the product and format, a 1 Gb/s encoder might generate several hundred megabits per second. Never use the Ethernet port speed as the assumed stream rate; obtain the manufacturer’s maximum media bitrate for the actual resolution and mode.

### Heavier compression

H.264, H.265 and similar codecs can reduce video to tens of megabits per second—or less—but normally introduce more encoding delay and can visibly degrade difficult material.

These are useful for:

- Signage
- Recording
- Remote contribution
- Streaming
- Large-scale distribution where ultra-low latency is unnecessary

Codec selection is therefore an architectural choice involving image quality, latency, bandwidth and interoperability.

---

## 3. Unicast versus multicast

### Unicast: one sender, one receiver

A unicast transmission has a specific destination.

If an 800 Mb/s encoder sends independently to six decoders, it may need to transmit six copies:


```text
800 Mb/s × 6 = 4.8 Gb/s
```


That is impossible through a 1 Gb/s encoder port.

Unicast is simple and often sensible when only one or a few receivers need a source.

### Multicast: one sender, a receiver group

A multicast sender transmits one copy addressed to a multicast group. The network replicates it where paths branch toward interested receivers.

With properly operating IGMP snooping:

- The encoder sends one 800 Mb/s stream.
- Each link that needs the group carries one copy.
- A switch replicates the stream onto receiver-facing ports.
- Adding receivers on an existing branch does not require additional copies from the encoder.

This is the fundamental scaling advantage of multicast.

But multicast is not magically free:

- Every receiver port still carries the complete stream.
- Each uplink carrying the group consumes its full bitrate.
- Separate downstream branches each need a copy.
- Without IGMP snooping, switches may flood the traffic.
- Without a working querier, membership state can age out or behave unpredictably.

Audinate similarly distinguishes Dante unicast and multicast flows: multicast does not require additional sender bandwidth as receivers are added, but it can consume bandwidth across links where it propagates. ([dev.audinate.com](https://dev.audinate.com/GA/dante-controller/userguide/webhelp/content/routing_media.htm), [dev.audinate.com](https://dev.audinate.com/GA/dante-controller/userguide/webhelp/content/fanout.htm))

### Important distinction: switching versus routing

An AV operator may say, “Route Encoder 4 to Decoder 12.”

That does not necessarily mean an IP router is involved. The control system may merely tell Decoder 12 to leave one multicast group and join another. Ethernet switches then change where the multicast frames are forwarded.

AV routing and Layer 3 IP routing are related words describing different operations.

---

## 4. The functional planes

These are useful design categories, even when a product combines them on one port or VLAN.

| Plane | Purpose | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Media | Real-time audio, video or USB payload | RTP, Dante audio, multicast video |
| AV control | Discovery, subscriptions and routing commands | Device discovery, source selection, API commands |
| Management | Configuration, monitoring and maintenance | HTTPS, SSH, SNMP, syslog, firmware |
| Timing | Common clock reference | PTP |

The planes do not automatically require four VLANs. They may share one network, or a product may allow some to be separated.

The documentation should nevertheless identify each function because they have different requirements:

- Media needs bandwidth and consistent delivery.
- Control must reach the correct devices and servers.
- Management needs secure administrator access.
- Timing needs predictable behavior and the correct PTP domain.

ST 2110 intentionally separates elementary video, audio and data streams, then uses PTP to keep them aligned. ([smpte.org](https://www.smpte.org/standards/st2110)) A system can therefore have perfectly healthy media links but fail because the control server is unreachable—or have functional control pages while packet loss destroys the video.

---

## 5. Bandwidth exists at several places

Do not calculate only the total number of encoders. Calculate every potential bottleneck.

### Endpoint port

Can the encoder’s port carry its maximum output? Can a decoder receive all required simultaneous streams?

### Access-switch capacity

How many sources enter the switch? How many receiver copies leave it? Switches normally advertise large switching capacities, but confirm the actual model and installed modules.

### Uplinks

Suppose ten encoders each generate 850 Mb/s:


```text
10 × 850 Mb/s = 8.5 Gb/s
```


A 10 Gb/s uplink may technically pass that traffic, but it leaves limited room for packet overhead, bursts, other services or future additions.

If that link fails over to a 1 Gb/s backup, the topology is redundant only in the most decorative sense.

### Core, stack and ring paths

Determine the worst credible traffic direction after:

- An uplink failure
- A stack-member failure
- A spanning-tree topology change
- A ring operating through its remaining side
- Multiple receivers selecting different sources

The failure path must carry the required load, not merely establish link lights.

### Link aggregation

Two 10 Gb/s links in a LAG can provide 20 Gb/s of aggregate capacity, but a single stream is normally assigned to one physical member according to a hash.

A LAG does not generally turn one 12 Gb/s stream into two neat 6 Gb/s halves. It distributes different conversations across members, sometimes unevenly.

---

## 6. Commercial-AV examples

### Example 1: Visionary Solutions Duet with VLAN tagging

The Duet encoder scenario we discussed is a good example of multiple logical functions sharing one physical switch connection.

With its VLAN features configured, the endpoint can place different traffic onto separate tagged VLANs—for example:

- PacketAV video
- Dante/AES67 audio
- The expansion Ethernet port

The connected switch port must be configured as a tagged member of the corresponding VLANs using matching VLAN IDs.

With tagging disabled, those functions occupy one untagged network. That can prevent Dante from living on BMT’s preferred audio VLAN and can place a device connected to the expansion port directly into the video network.

This is not merely organization. An exposed expansion port could give a rogue or accidental device access to the AVoIP VLAN.

The drawing should show the endpoint as a **tag-aware multi-service endpoint**, not as an ordinary access-port device.

### Example 2: Compressed-video access switches and a Ruckus core

Imagine eight encoders producing 750 Mb/s each on one ICX access switch:


```text
8 × 750 Mb/s = 6 Gb/s
```


A 10 Gb/s uplink to the core is reasonable for the present load.

Twelve decoders on another access switch can all watch one source. With multicast, its uplink carries approximately 750 Mb/s—not 9 Gb/s—because the receiving switch replicates the stream locally.

But if the twelve decoders select eight different sources, that receiver-switch uplink may carry all eight streams: approximately 6 Gb/s.

Receiver count alone does not determine uplink usage. The important value is the number of **distinct streams required across that link**.

---

## BMT standards takeaway

Every AVoIP riser should identify:

- Endpoint link speed
- Maximum stream bitrate and codec mode
- Unicast or multicast behavior
- Multicast group strategy
- VLAN for media, control, management and timing
- Normal and failure-path uplink loads
- IGMP snooping and querier location
- PTP domain and clock path
- LAG membership and limitations
- USB traffic, when transported
- Required bandwidth headroom
- Who owns each network configuration

The cloud can remain on the overview drawing—but the engineering sheets must explain what happens inside it.

## Practical exercise

A system has six 800 Mb/s encoders on Switch A and twelve decoders on Switch B. The switches have a 10 Gb/s connection.

Calculate the A-to-B traffic when:

1. All twelve decoders watch Encoder 1 using multicast.
2. The decoders collectively watch all six encoders using multicast.
3. Encoder 1 sends twelve independent unicast copies.
4. The 10 Gb/s link fails over to 1 Gb/s.

Then identify which condition cannot operate as designed.

## Compact glossary

- **Codec:** Method used to encode and possibly compress media.
- **Stream:** Logical media transmission.
- **Unicast:** One sender to one destination.
- **Multicast:** One sender to a receiver group.
- **Plane:** Conceptual category of system traffic.
- **RTP:** Real-time Transport Protocol.
- **Oversubscription:** Potential traffic exceeds available link capacity.
- **LAG:** Link Aggregation Group.
- **Headroom:** Unused capacity reserved for overhead, bursts and growth.

## Review questions

1. Why does multicast reduce sender bandwidth but not receiver-port bandwidth?  
2. What determines the load on an uplink serving multicast receivers?  
3. Why can a two-link LAG still fail to carry one exceptionally large stream?

### Answers

1. The sender transmits one group-addressed copy, but every receiver must still receive the complete stream.  
2. The combined bitrate of the distinct multicast groups needed across that uplink—not simply the number of receivers.  
3. A single flow is normally hashed onto one member rather than divided packet-by-packet across both links.

## Where we are headed

We now have the overall AVoIP architecture. **Lesson 20 will dissect Dante and AES67:** channels versus flows, unicast and multicast subscriptions, PTP clock election, latency settings, primary/secondary networks and what AES67 interoperability actually does—and does not—guarantee.
